theme: Those who go down to the sea
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 107:23-43. Here are the sailors in the storm, and then a series of reversals in which God turns deserts into pools and the proud into the humble. Notice how the psalm ends with a wisdom saying.
settingTheScene: This is the second half of Psalm 107, which you began five days ago. The first half told of wanderers, prisoners, and the sick. This half begins with the sailors and then moves to a hymn of reversals. It is a fitting close to the story of Jeremiah’s siege and fall, since it shows God as the one who humbles the proud and lifts the lowly. The psalm will return again later in the plan.
observation: “Some went down to the sea in ships, doing business on the great waters” (v. 23).
“They saw the deeds of the LORD, his wondrous works in the deep” (v. 24).
“He commanded and raised the stormy wind, which lifted up the waves of the sea” (v. 25).
“They reeled and staggered like drunken men and were at their wits” end’ (v. 27).
“Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still” (vv. 28-29).
“Then they were glad that need be still, and he brought them to their desired haven” (v. 30).
“He turns rivers into a desert, springs of water into thirsty ground” (v. 33).
“Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things; let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD” (v. 43).
interpretation:
The sailors are the fourth group. Unlike the others, they are not in trouble by sin or by accident. They are doing their work, “doing business on the great waters,” and a storm comes. God himself “commanded and raised the stormy wind.” This reminds us that not all trouble is a punishment for sin. Sometimes God brings storms to show his deeds in the deep. The sailors reel like drunks and their courage melts. They are at their wits’ end, literally, “all their wisdom was swallowed up.” Then they cry out, and he stills the storm to a whisper. The haven they long for is his gift.

From verse 33, the psalm shifts to a broader picture of God’s rule. He turns rivers into deserts and deserts into pools. The change depends on the moral condition of the people: a fruitful land becomes salt because of the wickedness of its inhabitants. And he settles the hungry in a desert turned to pools. He blesses them so that they multiply. This is God’s rule of reversal: he brings princes into contempt and lifts the needy out of affliction and makes their families like flocks.

The statement in verse 42 is clear: “The upright see it and are glad, and all wickedness shuts its mouth.” The psalm closes with a wisdom call. “Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things.” The wise person reads history and life as the story of God’s steadfast love. In the context of the exile, the lesson is that the return will be a work of God, in the same pattern of rescue after crying out.

All four of the psalm’s stories describe the same truth: when we are at our wits’ end, we can cry out to the LORD, and he hears.
connection: Jesus calmed the storm with a word: “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39), and the disciples asked, “Who then is this?” Psalm 107:29 gives the answer: the LORD. Jesus walked on water (Matthew 14:22-33). Luke 1:52-53 echoes the reversals: he has brought down the mighty and exalted the humble. 2 Corinthians 1:8-10 describes being so utterly burdened that we despaired of life, and God delivering us.
application:
Think about a storm you are in. Pray, “Lord, I am at my wits” end,’ and ask him to still it.

Consider that not every storm is a punishment. Look for what God may be showing you in it.

Take time to “attend to these things” by reviewing the rescues of this psalm, and thank God.
prayerPrompts: Tell God about the storm you are in and that you are at your wits’ end.
Ask him to bring you to your desired haven.
Thank Jesus, who stilled the storm.
